Śatadūṣaṇī
(‘[a work pointing out] a hundred defects [in Advaita Vedānta]’)
------------------------------------------
Offence is the best form of defence! This principle seems to have inspired a number of scholars of the various schools of Vedānta to produce highly polemical works with a view to demolishing other, rival, systems.
One such work is the Śatadūṣaṇī of वेदान्त देशिक (A.

-1370). It has been commented upon by Rāmānujadāsa and Śrīnivāsācarya. These commentaries are known as Caṇḍamāruta and Sahasra-kiraṇī.
Though the title indicates one hundred refutations of Advaita Vedānta of शङ्कर (A.

-820) the text now available has only sixty-six. Scholars opine that the rest of the work comprising thirty four refutations might have been lost or the work might have ended with the sixty sixth paragraph only. In that case ‘śata’ may mean, not ‘hundred’, but ‘many’.
It is interesting to note that वेदान्त देशिक considers Śāṅkara Vedānta’s barring of शूद्रस् from attaining the knowledge of ब्रह्मन्, as inappropriate.
The work concludes with the statement that शङ्कर’s philosophy cannot be reconciled with that of the Brahmasūtras.
See VEDĀNTA DEŚIKA also.

Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa
------------------------------------------
The biggest of all the ब्राह्मणस्, the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa belongs to the Śukla Yajurveda. It derives its name from the fact that it has śata or one hundred chapters.
It might have been compiled during 3000 B. C. It is available in two शाखास् or recensions: the Kāṇva and the Mādhyan-dina. The Kāṇvaśākhā has 17 kāṇḍas (books) divided into 104 adhyāyas (chapters). They are subdivided into 435 ब्राह्मणस् (subsections), the total number of kaṇḍikās or mantras being 6806.
The corresponding figures for the Mādhyandinaśākhā are 14; 100; 438 and 7624.
It may be interesting to note that the first nine kāṇḍas of the Mādhyandina recension follow the Saṁhitā (the Śukla यजुर्वेद Saṁhitā, also called the Vājasaneyī Saṁhitā) closely. They may be considered like a commentary.
The work, almost entirely, concerns itself with the various aspects of वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्.
A very brief summary of the contents may now be given:
Kāṇḍa 1
Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice.
Kāṇḍa 2
Agnyādhāna (producing the sacrificial fire); अग्निहोत्र; पिण्डपितृयज्ञ (sacrifice to the manes); आग्रयण (offering of first fruits) and चातुर्मास्य (four-monthly sacrifices).
Kāṇḍas 3 and 4
Somayāga.
Kāṇḍa 5
Vājapeya and राजसूय sacrifices.
Kāṇḍas 6 to 10
Viṣṇukrama (taking three or four steps in a सोमयाग with mantras of विष्णु); vaṇī-वाहन (coming and going of the vessel containing fire on a cart); cayana (piling of fire); Śatarudrīyahoma (homa with the mantras of the Rudrā-dhyāya); upāsanā (meditation) on अग्नि and a few other topics.
Kāṇḍas 11 to 14
Upanayana; ब्रह्मयज्ञ (Vedic studies); obsequial rites; अश्वमेध; Sarvamedha; पुरुषमेध and प्रवर्ग्य (a minor rite associated with सोमयाग).
There is very little difference of topics in the Kāṇva recension.
The sage याज्ञवल्क्य is prominent in the first five kāṇḍas. However, it is the sage शाण्डिल्य that is very conspicuous in the next five. Even then, all the ten kāṇḍas must have been the handiwork of Yājñnavalkya who gave शाण्डिल्य his due place out of respect.
The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa mentions by name many janapadas or countries such as गान्धार, Kekaya, Śālva, certain parts of आर्यावर्त, Kurupāñcāla, कोसल, Videha and Sṛñjaya.
Apart from describing many वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् in great detail, the work also gives many interesting ākhyānas or stories of the ancient periods often with historical content.
There is an obvious reference to the spread of Vedic religion and culture from the river सरस्वती in the west right up to the river Sadānīrā (Sarayū?) in the east.
Spiritual interpretations of the sacrifices also find a place now and then.
The root of the story of मत्स्यावतार (Fish-इन्चर्नतिओन्) and jalapralaya or water-deluge are also recorded here.
On the whole it can safely be declared that this Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa is one of the few and most important works of the Vedic literature.
See also YAJURVEDA.

satkāryavāda
(‘the theory of the effect really existing [previously in the cause]’)
------------------------------------------
Since a real effect cannot come out of an unreal cause, this theory put forward by the Sāṅkhya philosophy argues that the effect (‘kārya’) must have pre-existed (‘sat’) in the cause, in a subtle form before manifestation. This is सत्कार्यवाद. This theory is also called आरम्भवाद and परिणामवाद.
See also ASATKĀRYAVĀDA.

Satyabhāmā
------------------------------------------
Satyabhāmā was one of the aṣṭa-mahiṣīs or eight queens of कृष्ण. She was the daughter of Satrājit, a chieftain of the यदु race.
In her previous life she was Guṇavatī, daughter of a pious ब्राह्मण Deva-śarman. Due to her purity of life, austerities and devotion to विष्णु, she was reborn as सत्यभामा and got Kṛṣna as her husband.
It was for fulfilling her wish, that कृष्ण brought the पारिजात (night jasmine) tree from हेअवेन्.
Once she was obliged to accept defeat at the hands of रुक्मिणी, the chief queen of कृष्ण, whose devotion proved to be greater than hers.

Śatarudriya
------------------------------------------
Japa or repetition of Vedic mantras or passages is said to purify a person. One of such well-known passages is the Rudra or the Rudrādhyāya (Taittirīya Saṁhitā 4.5.1-11).
Since the Yajurveda has 102 शाखास् or recensions and since this Rudra appears in all of them, it has been designated as Śatarudriya (śata = one hundred) also.
See RUDRAPRAŚNA.

Śatrughna
(‘one who kills or destroys the enemy’)
------------------------------------------
Śatrughna was a son of सुमित्रा, the second queen of दशरथ. He and Lakṣmana were twins. He was very much attached to भरत, even as लक्ष्मण was to राम.
Very little is mentioned about him in the first six books of वाल्मीकि’s Rāmāyaṇa.
He was married to Śrutakīrti, daughter of Kuśadhvaja, younger brother of जनक.
He was sent to मथुरा by राम to kill the demon-king Lavaṇāsura who had become a despot and terror to his subjects. He not only killed Lavaṇāsura but also took over the kingdom as its ruler and ruled it according to the highest principles of धर्म.
Since he had not seen राम for a long time he visited the hermitage of वाल्मीकि and then came to अयोध्या, after dividing his kingdom between his two sons Subāhu and Śatrughāti who ruled from मथुरा and Vaidiśa respectively.
Rāma was extremely happy to meet him.
When राम decided to go back to his divine abode, शत्रुघ्न too followed him.

satpratipakṣa
(‘inferentially contradicted middle’)
------------------------------------------
The well-known example given for अनुमान or inference in the Indian systems of लोगिच् like the न्याय दर्शन runs as follows:
There is fire on the yonder hill;
because there is smoke.
Wherever there is smoke, there is fire.
There are three factors here. They are called पक्ष (minor term, the hill), साध्य (major term, the fire) and लिङ्ग or हेतु (middle term, the smoke).
However, an inference can be falla-cious—this is called hetvābhāsa—and it is of five types. The सत्प्रतिपक्ष is the third in the series. Here, the middle term is contradicted by another statement which is sat or real.
Suppose the first statement is:
Sound is eternal, because it is audible.
This is contradicted by a second one thus:
Sound is non-eternal because it is produced, like a pot.
Here, the non-existence of eternality in the first is proved by the second inference (which is a pratipakṣa or opposition view) which is sat or real.
See HETVĀBHĀSA also.

sattva
(‘existence’)
------------------------------------------
Used in several senses such as purity and strength, this word represents सत्त्व-गुण, the first of the three guṇas.
The Chāndogya Upaniṣad (7.26.2) has used it in the sense of the मिन्द्.
See GUṆA.

Śātātapa
------------------------------------------
Śātātapa is one of the ancient authors of a स्मृति, quoted by others like याज्ञवल्क्य, पराशर, विश्वरूप and हरदत्त, especially on the topic of प्रायश्चित्त or expiations for sins.
His work seems to have been both in prose and in verses. Or, the prose-work in the form of sūtras and the one in verses may have been different compilations.
The manuscript of a Śātātapa Smṛti discovered, has twelve chapters dealing with the following subjects: prāyaścittas, विवाह (marriage), वैश्वदेव (offering of cooked ड़ोओद् for all gods, a domestic rite), śrāddha (obsequial rites), rules about taking ड़ोओद्, अशौच (observance of ceremonial impurities) and so on.
Another work called Karmavipāka attributed to शातातप contains different subjects like gifts of land, eulogy of ब्राह्मणस्, rites for those who meet violent or accidental death and certain penances.
One more work called Vṛddha-Śātātapa has also been quoted by the writers and commentators of धर्म-śāstras.

Satyavān
(‘the truthful one’)
------------------------------------------
See SĀVITRĪ.

Śatacaṇḍī
------------------------------------------
One of the most important texts of the शाक्त school (cult of the Divine मोथेर्) is the Caṇḍī, also known as the Devīmāhātmya or the Durgāsaptaśatī. A ceremonial recital of this work is believed to bestow on the devotee whatever boon he wants.
If ten ब्राह्मणस् of pure character recite it ten times it becomes शतचण्डी. If a hundred ब्राह्मणस् recite it ten times it becomes Sahasracaṇḍī. The recital is spread over four days as follows:
First day Once
Second day Two times
Third day Three times
Fourth day Four times

After the recital, a hundred brāh-maṇas are to be fed in the former and a thousand in the latter.
The शतचण्डी and the Sahasracaṇḍī are conducted for the good of the whole society or the world.
See also CAṆḌĪPĀṬHA.

Sātyaki
------------------------------------------
Sātyaki was the son of Satyaka, a chieftain of the यदु race. He was also known as Yuyudhāna.
Throughout his life he was a devoted friend of कृष्ण and अर्जुन. No love was lost between him and बलराम (Kṛṣṇa’s elder brother) who always sided with दुर्योधन.
He accompanied कृष्ण on all his major sojourns like attending the Rājāsūya sacrifice or the final peace mission.
Not only did he advocate war with the Kauravas, he also took active part in it as one of the seven commanders of the Pāṇḍava army.
He too perished in the internecine quarrels of the Yādavas at प्रभास along with others.

Satyanārāyaṇa-vrata
------------------------------------------
This is an extremely popular vrata (religious rite), almost all over the country, especially among the lower middle class people and women. It can be done on any day, preferably on Pūrṇimā, सङ्क्रान्ति or एकादशी days, the places being a temple, bank of a river, under the vaṭa or अश्वत्थ trees or in one’s own होउसे. The quantity of naivedya (food offering) is fixed at 1¼ (for e.g., 1.25 kgs). The ingredients of this special naivedya are: plantains, ghee, milk, wheat or rice flour, jaggery or sugar. They are all to be mixed up to prepare the naivedya. Apart from the elaborate worship of the deity, listening to the stories about the greatness of this vrata, keeping vigil the whole night with devotional songs and devotional dances are also recommended.

sat
(‘the existent’)
------------------------------------------
The two words ‘sat’ and ‘asat’ are frequently mentioned and discussed in Indian philosophical and religious works. If ‘sat’ stands for existence, unchanging reality, truth or the good, ‘asat’ represents all that is opposed to it; the non-existent, the transient, falsehood, evil and so on.
However, the word ‘asat’ is sometimes used in the उपनिषद्स् in the sense of the unmanifested state (vide Taittirīyopaniṣad 2.7) before च्रेअतिओन्, and the word ‘sat’ to denote its manifested state.

Satyavatī
------------------------------------------
She was the daughter of a king Uparicara Vasu of Cedi (a kingdom) but was brought up by a chieftain of fishermen.
The sage पराशर was once infatuated with her beauty and कृष्ण-द्वैपायन व्यास was born of their union.
She was later married to the king Śantanu from whom she got two sons: Citrāṅgada and Vicitravīrya. Both these princes however died young.
Then, since भीष्म (Śantanu’s first son) was not willing to beget children in the widows of Vicitravīrya by नियोग (See NIYOGA.) Satyavati ordered व्यास to do so.
Later on, she is said to have retired into a forest along with her two daughters-in-law, अम्बिका and Ambālikā.
Viśvāmitra’s sister and the मोथेर् of the sage जमदग्नि was also a सत्यवती. The queen of the king त्रिशङ्कु of the solar race was another सत्यवती.

Satyaloka
(‘world of Truth’)
------------------------------------------
See BRAHMALOKA.

Sātvata
(‘belonging to the Satvat tribe’)
------------------------------------------
Sātvata was a king of the यदु dynasty. He had seven sons: Bhaja, Bhaji, दिव्य, Vṛṣṇi, Devapṛṣṭha, Andhaka and Mahābhoja.
All men born in his dynasty were known as Sātvatas.
Śrī कृष्ण was a descendent of Vṛṣṇi.
Sātvata is also the name of a Vaiṣṇava work that preaches devotion to विष्णु. This is called Bhāgavatamata.

satya
(‘truth’)
------------------------------------------
Satya or truth has been accorded the pride of place among the virtues recommended to be cultivated by man. The Hindu as well as Jaina and Buddhist works wax eloquently over it. Its fundamental definition is ‘that which is un-affected by time, place and causation’. This simply means that ‘satya’ stands for God, the Absolute. In fact, several sahasra-nāmas (thousand names of God) use this word to denote God. As an extension of this meaning, anything that helps a man’s progress towards God, is सत्य.
In a more practical sense, सत्य is speaking the truth, consonance of thought and word. One should avoid speaking falsehood, partial truths and even unpleasant truths. Truth should be spoken in a sweet and pleasant way. Unpleasant truths, when they must be spoken, should be presented in a palatable manner.
In the ancient days if a person accused of a crime denied it, he was to prove his innocence by touching a red-hot iron! It was believed that if he was speaking the truth, truth itself would protect him (vide Chāndogyopaniṣad 6.16.1,2)
Asatya on the other hand, stands for all that is opposed to सत्य. It is what is untrue, unreal, evil and crooked.
Speaking असत्य has been permitted as an आपद्-धर्म (emergency situation), under extraordinary circumstances when one’s life is threatened by evil and unscrupulous persons.

Satyārthaprakāśa
(‘[a work] which brings out the truth’)
------------------------------------------
The Satyārthaprakāśa is the magnum opus of Svāmi Dayānanda सरस्वती (A.

-1883), a pioneer in the renaissance of हिन्दुइस्म् during the 19th century. He was the founder of the well-known Ārya-samāj. (See ĀRYASAMĀJ and DAYĀNANDA SARASVATĪ.)
A powerful work on general हिन्दुइस्म् written in Hindī language, it has 14 ullāsas or chapters, with a concluding section also, in which he has given his own views on the various principles of हिन्दुइस्म्.
A brief summary of the work may now be given here:
First Chapter
Various names of God are mentioned here with relevant quotations from the वेदस्.
Second Chapter
Along with certain Vedic rites connected with the birth of a child and some techniques of training and educating it, this chapter discounts the claims of astrologers who cast the होरोस्चोपे and ridicules the इग्नोरन्चे of people who believe in ghosts and evil spirits.
Third Chapter
After emphasising the need for good एदुचतिओन्, both for boys and for girls, the work explains in detail प्राणायाम, उपनयन, सन्ध्या, ब्रह्मचर्य (first stage of life) and methods of study.
Here the author forcefully advocates the study of the वेदस् by the शूद्रस् and women also.
Fourth Chapter
The topics dealt with in this chapter are: eight types of मर्रिअगे; certain सṁस्कारस् or sacraments like पुṁसवन; the पञ्चमहायज्ञस् or the five daily sacrifices; duties of a गृहस्थ or a householder; characteristics of a good student; criticism of Parāśarasmṛti.
Fifth Chapter
The two āśramas, वानप्रस्थ and सṁन्यास, are described here.
There is a clear declaration that only ब्राह्मणस् are eligible for सṁन्यास.
In this chapter, it is interesting to note, that the Manusmṛti has been quoted extensively.
Sixth Chapter
The entire chapter deals with political science in detail. The Manusmṛti is quoted profusely.
Seventh Chapter
The following subjects are dealt with in this section: ईश्वर, ब्रह्मन् or God, his nature (as formless and all-pervading) and his worship through prayer and meditation; denial of the theory that God incarnates; about the nature of the जीव or individual सोउल्; जीव and ब्रह्मन् are different though a little similarity exists; वेदस् were created by ईश्वर or God; Vedic Saṁhitās are the real वेदस् and supreme.
Eighth Chapter
The topic of this chapter is च्रेअतिओन्. There are three fundamental realities: ईश्वर or परमात्मन्; जीव or the individual souls; प्रकृति or nature.
Īśvara does the primary च्रेअतिओन् of the whole world using प्रकृति as the material. The जीव does his own, using the articles available in the world.
Creation is a continuous process.
Karma theory is supported.
Advaita theory of ब्रह्मन् alone being the material as well as the efficient cause (abhinna-निमित्त-upādāna-कारण) is rejected.
Ninth Chapter
The subjects dealt with in this chapter are: characteristics of knowledge and इग्नोरन्चे; rejection of the various views of the advaitins; मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन् of the जीव and his 24 special powers.
The mukta or the liberated सोउल् returns to this world after the end of parāntakāla (duration of Brahma’s life) (3 x 1013 years). In मुक्ति he enjoys the bliss of ब्रह्मन्, being established in ब्रह्मन् who is infinite or all-pervading, the जीव himself being aṇu or atomic in size.
Tenth Chapter
This section deals with several topics normally dealt with in the dharmaśāstra works such as सदाचार (good conduct), service to parents and elders, purity of ड़ोओद्, unity of all the varṇas, need to avoid ड़्लेस्ह्-एअतिन्ग्, eschewing intoxicating drinks and mutual love and respect among all varṇas.
Eleventh Chapter
This is the biggest section dealing with several, miscellaneous, topics. They are, briefly, as follows:
Greatness of the knowledge and wisdom in India; destruction of the true spirit of the ब्राह्मणस् leads to total destruction; true meaning of अनिमल् सच्रिड़िचेस् such as अश्वमेध, Gomedha or पुरुष-medha; criticism of śrāddha conception; criticism of the various stories of the पुराणस्; true nature of तपस् or austerity; mūrtipūjā shown as defective, including the worship of the various deities; pilgrimages decried; पुराणस् are not by व्यास; Bhāgavata considered as बोपदेव’s work and hence not authoritative; शूद्रस् and women can study the वेदस्; no belief in अस्त्रोलोग्य्; dānas or making gifts accepted; criticism of many other schools.
Twelfth Chapter
This entire chapter is devoted to a severe criticism of the schools of Cārvāka (materialism), Jaina and Bauddha which are against the Vedic religion.
Thirteenth Chapter
It deals with Judaism and brushes it aside as a religion sanctioning violence. It also criticises Christianity.
Fourteenth Chapter
This chapter is devoted to denunciation of Islam and the Korān. Several सुरस् are quoted and critically analysed.
The Philosophy of Dayānanda सरस्वती as Revealed in this Treatise
Since the author has been devastatingly critical of most of the schools of हिन्दुइस्म् it is necessary to know what exactly his own philosophy is. This he has done in the last section titled Svamantavya-Amantavya-Prakāśaḥ (revealing what is acceptable as also not acceptable to himself).
The following is a brief summary of the concepts:
Īśvara or God
Known as ब्रह्मा, Paramātma and a host of other names, He is Sat-Cit-आनन्द (Truth, चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् and Bliss). He is omniscient, omnipresent and all-powerful. He is the creator, endowed with all the blessed qualities.
Pramāṇas (Means of Knowledge)
The Saṁhita portions of the four वेदस् are the basic प्रमाणस्.
The other parts of the वेदस् like the ब्राह्मणस्, वेदाङ्गस् and the Upavedas are accepted in so far as they do not conflict with the Saṁhitās.
In addition, eight प्रमाणस् are accepted. They are: प्रत्यक्ष (direct perception); अनुमान (inference); शब्द (verbal testimony, the वेदस्); उपमान (comparison); अर्थापत्ति (postulation); अनुपलब्धि (non-perception); sambhava (possibility); ऐतिह्य (past history).
Dharma (Righteousness)
It is the code of conduct given by the वेदस् and not against the spirit of the वेदस्.
Jīva
The जीव or the individual सोउल् is नित्य (uncreated and eternal) and aṇu (atomic in size). He has several qualities like icchā (desire), द्वेष (dislike), prayatna (effort), ज्ञान (knowledge) and so on.
There are many jīvas. They are all different from ईश्वर, though similar in nature. ईश्वर being omnipresent, pervades them.
Prakṛti (Nature)
The world is created by ईश्वर using this प्रकृति as the material cause.
Sṛṣṭi (Creation)
Creation is done by ईश्वर to help the jīvas in their path of further evolution, according to their karmas.
Bandha (Bondage)
The जीव falls into bondage due to अविद्या or इग्नोरन्चे of his real nature.
Mukti (Liberation)
Mukti is लिबेरतिओन् from all sorrows and sufferings. The liberated सोउल् will get full freedom to move about in the whole च्रेअतिओन् as also in ईश्वर who is all-pervading. However, the liberated सोउल् has to come back at the end of a parāntakāla, the life duration of ब्रह्मा.
Īśvaropāsana (worship of God) through योग, विद्या (knowledge), practice of धर्म and company of the spiritually evolved souls, is the means.
Varṇāśramadharmas
They are accepted if based on गुण (qualities of the मिन्द्) and कर्म (actions in accordance with them) and not based on birth.
Devas and Asuras (Gods and Demons)
Vidvāṁsas (men of wisdom) are the देवस् (gods) and the avidvāṁsas (men of इग्नोरन्चे) are the असुरस्. Sinners are the राक्षसस् and renegades, the piśācis.
Devapūjā (Worship of God)
Honouring the men of wisdom, one’s own parents, the teacher, a just king, guests and virtuous persons—this is real देवपूजा.
Śikṣaṇa (Education)
The training that helps one to eliminate the impurities of the मिन्द् and develop great virtues is śikṣaṇa in the true sense.
Purāṇas
It is the ब्राह्मणस् of the वेदस् that are accepted as the पुराणस् and not the present eighteen पुराणस्.
Tīrthas (Places of पिल्ग्रिमगे)
It is the cultivation of virtues like truth, knowledge and the company of the spiritually great souls that is true ‘tīrtha’ and not the physical places of पिल्ग्रिमगे.
Puruṣaprayatna (Self-effort)
Even prārabdha कर्म can be overcome by purṣaprayatna.
Saṁskāra (Sacraments)
All the sixteen सṁस्कारस् are accepted. However, nothing need be done after च्रेमतिओन्.
Yajñas (Sacrifices)
Simple Vedic rituals are accepted but not the complicated system of sacrifices.
Āryas (Cultured People)
The word does not indicate any race. It refers to the cultured and refined people as against the दस्युस्, the evil ones.
Svarga and Naraka (Heaven and हेल्ल्)
The experience of joy and happiness here is स्वर्ग and the opposite is नरक.
Karma and Punarjanma (Karma and Rebirth)
The usual theories are accepted.
Niyoga (Levirate)
The ancient system of नियोग is accepted within the framework of the rules prescribed.
Upāsanā (worship and meditation), prārthanā (prayer) and yogābhyāsa are also accepted.
See also ĀRYASAMĀJ and DAYĀNANDA SARASVATĪ.

Satī
(‘the chaste one’)
------------------------------------------
Satī was a daughter of दक्ष प्रजापति given in मर्रिअगे to शिव.
Being a paragon of the highest womanly virtues and unable to bear the insults hurled at her husband by her arrogant ड़थेर् दक्ष, she burnt herself in a self-generated fire through योग in the sacrificial hall (of दक्ष). She was later reborn as पार्वती (the daughter of the mountain king Himavān and queen Menā) and married शिव after pleasing him with severe austerities.
Because of this act of hers, her name—Satī—became a synonym for pātivratya or chastity and absolute faithfulness to one’s husband.
See also PĀRVATĪ.
